title: A Microfluidic Platform for Precision Small-volume Sample Processing and Its Use to Size Separate Biological Particles with an Acoustic Microdevice
protocol: Lay out Mask 1, the Fluidic Layer (front side), using appropriate CAD software.
Choose a geometry that permits sample injection and separation appropriate for the desired application.

Set the fluidic channel width w to provide a resonant frequency fn greater than 1 MHz according to the equation fn = nc/2w, where c is the speed of sound in the relevant fluid and n is the number of standing-wave nodes.
Particles occupying distinct lateral positions near the end of the separation channel should exit from distinct outlets.
Set the fluid channel length to control the length of time particles are exposed to the separation field at a specific flow rate.
Pattern the back-side fluid ports using Mask 2 on a double-side polished 0.5-mm thick, 100-mm diameter <100> silicon wafer by standard positive-resist photolithography.
Etch the geometry by deep reactive ion etching (DRIE) to a depth of 350–400 µm.
Turn the wafer over and pattern the front-side fluid channel geometry using Mask 1 by standard positive-resist photolithography onto the other side of the silicon.
Mount the device wafer to a second blank silicon carrier wafer using photoresist.
Etch the channels, also by DRIE, to a depth of 200 µm, through-etching the silicon in the port locations.
De-mount the device wafer from the blank Si wafer by soaking in resist-stripping solution.
Clean the device wafer and a featureless 0.5 mm-thick borosilicate glass wafer using Piranha solution (sulfuric acid and hydrogen peroxide in a 3:1 ratio).

Seal the fluid channels by anodically bonding the glass and silicon wafers at chamber pressure of 3 mTorr, piston pressure of 1,000 N, temperature of 350 °C, and apply 750 V until the current drops below 0.2 mA.
Cut the individual chips apart with a diamond blade on a dicing saw.
Weigh out the recommended ratio of both components from a two-component low-viscosity epoxy kit.
Mix the weighed components thoroughly.
Dispense approximately 10 µl of the epoxy mixture across a lead zirconate titanate (PZT) piezoceramic using a pipette.
Spread the epoxy mixture evenly across the piezoceramic to create a thin, even layer.
Align the epoxy side of the piezoceramic with the microfluidic chip using a suitable jig or fixture, ensuring an overhanging area on one side for wire attachment.
Bring the aligned components into contact carefully.
Clamp the assembly in a vice without cracking any components.
Cure the assembly at the temperature and duration recommended by the epoxy manufacturer.
Attach fine-gauge wire leads to each side of the piezoceramic using soldering with a fine-tip soldering iron, making brief contact to avoid thermal depolarization.
Alternatively, use conductive adhesive to glue wires to the piezo.
Attach the chip to the fluidic breadboard using clamping fixtures.
Attach a cooling fan to the breadboard to regulate temperature during acoustic experiments.
Screw in chip-to-world connectors.
Join interface tubes to additional tubing at the inlets and outlets using standard ¼”-28 unions for 1/16” tubing.
Assemble the microfluidic chip using world-to-chip connections on the fluidic breadboard.
Connect tubing (such as 1/16” outer diameter fluoropolymer tubing) to a fluid pump and collection vials.
Mount the breadboard assembly on the stage of a microscope capable of fluorescence imaging equipped with a CCD camera.
Connect lengths of small inner diameter (ID) tubing (0.006”) immediately after the chip to serve as flow restrictors.
Use larger ID tubes, such as 0.01” or 0.03”, for all other connections.
Estimate the hydrodynamic flow resistance Rh for each piece of tubing using the equation Rh = 128 μL/πD4.
Calculate the pressure drop ΔP due to each length of tubing at a given flow rate Q using ΔP = QRh.
Choose a ratio of restrictor lengths to split the flow between the outlets as appropriate for the separation method being used.
Optimal separation with the acoustic chips in this protocol requires an SPO:LPO flow ratio of approximately 65:35%.
Choose the length of the outlet flow restrictors such that their fluidic resistance is at least 3–4 times larger than the total resistance in the rest of the system.
For the acoustophoresis device used in this work, use tubing lengths of 35 cm for LPO and 65 cm for SPO.
Check for leaks to verify that the microfluidic device has no defects and all tubing connections are sealed.
Dispense water through the inlet tubes with a syringe and monitor for any fluid leaking in the main channel.
Dispense a known volume through the chip and measure the volumes collected from the outlets to ensure the flow ratio is as expected.
Flush the entire system (fluidic tubing and chip) with appropriate cleaning solutions before running experiments.
Flush the entire system (fluidic tubing and chip) with appropriate cleaning solutions after running experiments.
Plug the clear outlet and flush the system if there are clogs or blockages in one of the outlets.
Reverse the flow direction during flushing while applying rapid pulses of reverse flow using a manually-actuated syringe, if necessary.
Replace the tubing or chip if the blockage cannot be removed by reversing the flow direction.
Fill the bypass channel with deionized water, ethanol, or phosphate buffered saline (PBS) using a syringe.
Prepare a bead solution containing approximately 0.01% (w/v) fluorescent polymer beads (5-8 µm) suspended in PBS with 0.05% Tween-20.
Fill the sample inlet syringe with the bead solution.
Fill the buffer inlet syringe with PBS with 0.05% Tween-20.
Focus halfway into the depth of the channel at a straight region just before the outlet on the microscope stage.
Ensure both channels (separation and bypass) are in the field of view for imaging.
Make electrical connections using shielded cables equipped with BNC connectors to a function generator with an RF amplifier.
Connect an oscilloscope to the output of the function generator for monitoring voltage.
Turn on the cooling fan.
Set the function generator output to 12–25 volts peak-to-peak (Vpp) for the piezo transducer.
Set both syringes to the same flow rate between 50 and 200 µl/min.
Perform a frequency scan procedure by specifying start, end frequencies, and step size.
Apply voltage at each frequency step for 15 seconds to allow system equilibration.
Capture 10 images of beads flowing through the chip at each step.
Turn off the voltage between steps for approximately 20 seconds to redistribute beads uniformly.
Run an image analysis script such as AF_freqScanPlotter.m.
Select the list of image files generated in Step 4.4.
Enter the scan start and stop frequencies and step size.
Enter the full channel width.
Enter the wall location.
Select the image region to analyze, including both the separation and bypass channels.
Observe the analysis script average the set of images captured at each frequency step.
Observe the analysis script average the intensity values along the flow direction.
This results in a cross-section line-scan of fluorescence intensity.
Use a sample buffer suitable for the cells or particles to be separated.
Ensure that the recovery buffer matches the sample fluid as required by the analysis assay.
Mix any necessary buffers and samples in preparation for separation.
Configure the acoustic system according to the specified setup for automated experiments.
Ensure cleaning reagent reservoirs (bleach, ethanol, buffer) are filled adequately.
Verify waste reservoirs are not full.
Prime fluid lines with solution.
Run automated cleaning procedure if uncertain or first use after idle period.
Set Valves 3 and 4 to flow to waste reservoirs initially.
Turn on the cooling fan.
Set function generator at resonant frequency for the acoustic chip being used.
Adjust voltage set point so RF amplifier outputs between 12 and 25 Vpp.
Connect Sample Input Vial, Buffer Input Vial, and appropriate collection vials to system.
Vortex the Sample Input Vial briefly before attachment to re-suspend particles.
Attach the Sample Input Vial to pickup tubing immediately after vortexing.
Initiate separation routine without delay.
Prime the pickup tubing.
Withdraw approximately 15 µl from the Sample Input Vial to completely fill the tube connecting it to Valve 1.
Simultaneously, prime the tube connecting the Buffer Input Vial to Valve 2.
Prime the air inlet of Valve 1 to ensure that it contains no fluid.
Switch Valves 1 and 2 to expel to waste any excess fluid or air that has entered the loading coil.
Load the sample coil as described in Figure 5a.
Withdraw 25 µl of air at 50 µl/min.
Withdraw 250 µl of sample at 200 µl/min.
Withdraw 35 µl of leading buffer at 200 µl/min.
Withdraw another 25 µl of air at 50 µl/min.
Set the syringe pumps to infuse the loaded fluid plugs at the desired rate (typically 100 µl/min).
Monitor the flow rates at the SPO and LPO with flow sensors to ensure steady flow and correct ratio.
Switch the corresponding output valve from waste when a spike in flow rate is detected, indicating passage of the first air gap.
Observe the flow sensor detect the second air gap.
Switch the output valves back to waste.
Stop the syringe pump infusion when the flow rate reaches zero.
Disconnect the SPO and LPO sample collection vials after separation is complete.
Secure the SPO, LPO, and sample pickup tubes in empty vials for cleaning solutions.
Start the automated system cleaning routine.
Flush the holding coil with 450 μl of 10% bleach.
Flush the holding coil with 450 μl of 70% ethanol.
End the flush sequence with 1,000 μl of water or appropriate saline buffer.
Flush each reagent into the SPO while the LPO outlet valve is set to a port that is blocked.
Then flush each reagent into the LPO while the SPO outlet valve is set to a port that is blocked.
Maintain withdrawal and infusion flow rates of 300–500 µl/min to minimize bubble generation in the tubing and backpressure buildup when either the SPO or the LPO is blocked.
Discard excess flushing solutions following appropriate procedures for handling biological or chemical waste.
